notes: Ruling slot 1 must hold President Pacheco Areco's Colorado Party, so the Colorados move from MD slot 2 to 1 (keeping their own sprite URG_western_liberal) and the Blancos take coalition slot 2 with their sprite URG_western_conservative; there is no formal coalition, Pacheco relies on ad hoc Blanco votes. Herrerism (Blanco right) in 6, Jorge Batlle's List 15 in 16, Michelini's List 99 in 3. Frente Amplio added as 1971.2.5 second period of slot 18 after the banned Socialist Party, which co-founded it.

0.name: Los pachequistas
0.text:
The pachequistas are the inner circle of President Jorge Pacheco Areco: businessmen-ministers, police chiefs and loyal Colorado bosses who have governed under the Prompt Security Measures almost without pause since June 1968. They froze wages and prices, militarised striking public employees and closed left-wing newspapers.

They see Uruguay at war with subversion and want a strong executive above a quarrelsome parliament. Firmly aligned with Washington, they welcome American police advisers of the Office of Public Safety. Their leverage lies in presidential decree powers, control of the police and the fear of the Tupamaros among the middle classes.

1.name: Partido Colorado
1.text:
The Colorado Party, the party of José Batlle y Ordóñez and of the Uruguayan welfare state, has governed again since 1967. President Jorge Pacheco Areco, who succeeded the late Óscar Gestido in December 1967, now rules under emergency measures, while the party is split into rival lists from the conservative pachequistas to the left-wing Batllistas.

Pacheco's government stands for order, wage restraint and stabilisation against inflation and the Tupamaro insurgency, close ties to the United States and a firm hand with the unions. Its leverage lies in state patronage, Montevideo's party clubs and the electoral law that pools votes across all Colorado lists.

2.name: Partido Nacional
2.text:
The National Party, the Blancos, is Uruguay's other historic party and the main opposition since losing power in 1966. Rooted in the countryside and the memory of caudillos such as Aparicio Saravia, it is divided between a conservative Herrerist wing and a rising reformist current around Senator Wilson Ferreira Aldunate.

It defends rural interests, decentralisation and national sovereignty, but its reformers increasingly attack Pacheco's emergency rule and call for agrarian reform and a cleaner state. Pro-Western yet suspicious of Washington's tutelage, its leverage lies in its rural electorate, its seats in parliament and the votes Pacheco needs to pass his laws.

3.name: Movimiento por el Gobierno del Pueblo – Lista 99
3.english: Movement for the Government of the People
3.native_full: Movimiento por el Gobierno del Pueblo – Lista 99
3.text:
The Movement for the Government of the People, known as List 99, is the left-wing Batllista faction of the Colorado Party led by Senator Zelmar Michelini. Founded in 1962, it broke with Pacheco over the emergency measures and the repression of unions and students, and now acts as a dissident opposition within the governing party.

It stands for the old Batllista welfare state renewed by planning, agrarian reform, civil liberties and an independent foreign policy. Its base lies among Montevideo's public employees, teachers and young professionals, and its leverage comes from Michelini's oratory and his bridges to the wider left.

4.name: Partido Comunista del Uruguay
4.text:
The Communist Party of Uruguay, led by Rodney Arismendi, is the strongest Moscow-aligned party in South America outside Chile. Legal but harassed under the emergency measures, it contests elections through the Leftist Liberation Front (FIdeL) and dominates the National Convention of Workers, the unified trade union centre.

It pursues a broad anti-imperialist and anti-oligarchic front with progressive Colorados, Blancos and Christian Democrats, rejects the guerrilla road of the Tupamaros and follows the Soviet line closely. Its leverage lies in disciplined cadres, the unions' power to paralyse the country and its newspaper El Popular.

5.name: Movimiento de Liberación Nacional – Tupamaros
5.text:
The National Liberation Movement – Tupamaros is the urban guerrilla organisation founded in the mid-1960s around Raúl Sendic, a former Socialist organiser of the northern sugar-cane workers. In 1969 it robbed banks and casinos, exposed financial scandals, kidnapped prominent figures and briefly seized the town of Pando, becoming the most famous urban guerrilla in the world.

It seeks a socialist revolution through armed struggle, holding that Uruguay's democracy is a façade for the oligarchy and American imperialism. Its leverage lies in clandestine cells in Montevideo, sympathy among students and young professionals, and the government's inability to break it.

6.name: Herrerismo
6.text:
Herrerism is the conservative nationalist wing of the National Party founded by Luis Alberto de Herrera, who dominated the Blancos for half a century until his death in 1959. It is now led by Martín Echegoyen and draws on cattle ranchers, rural towns and Catholic traditionalists.

It defends property, order and the Hispanic Catholic heritage, distrusts Batllista statism and urban radicals alike, and keeps Herrera's stubborn hostility to foreign tutelage, from American bases to Pan-American interventionism. Its leverage lies in the Blanco rural vote, its weight in parliament and its friends in the officer corps.

7.name: Los peruanistas
7.text:
The peruanistas are junior and middle-ranking officers who admire the revolutionary military government of General Juan Velasco Alvarado in Peru. Drawn into the fight against the Tupamaros, they have begun to read the guerrillas' exposés of bank fraud and corruption and to blame the politicians and the oligarchy for the country's crisis.

They imagine an army that would clean up the state, nationalise the banks, carry out land reform and break with American economic tutelage. They have no public leader and no organisation beyond barracks conversations, but their leverage could become decisive if the armed forces enter politics.

8.name: Ahl al-Bayt de Montevideo
8.text:
The Montevideo Ahl al-Bayt Circle gathers a few Lebanese Shia families, shopkeepers and travelling merchants who meet in private homes for Ashura and religious feasts. Most arrived from southern Lebanon over the past decades and have integrated into Uruguayan commercial life.

They follow from afar Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon, and share his message of dignity and peaceful advancement for the Shia poor. Apolitical in Uruguay, they wield no influence beyond their families and trade.

9.name: Halqat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a handful of devout young Lebanese Shia in Montevideo and the border town of Chuy who read sermons sent from the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini teaches. They keep to themselves and are unknown to Uruguayan politics.

They hold that Muslims should be governed by the learned clergy, and they reject both American power and atheist communism. In Uruguay they have no weight at all; their significance lies only in their correspondence with radical clerical networks in Lebanon and Iraq.

10.name: Musalla del Chuy
10.text:
The Chuy Prayer Room is the gathering place of Palestinian and Syrian merchants who run shops in the duty-free border town of Chuy and in Montevideo's commercial districts. Pious and practical, they keep their faith alive with a modest prayer room, Qur'an lessons and support from the Muslim World League in Mecca.

They are conservative, respectful of authority and avoid Uruguayan politics, looking to the Gulf monarchies as guardians of the faith. Their small influence rests on trade, savings and the respect they enjoy along the Brazilian border.

11.name: Halqat al-Umma
11.text:
The Umma Circle is a tiny group of young Palestinians in Chuy and Montevideo, embittered by the defeat of 1967, who circulate pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir obtained through relatives in Jordan and Lebanon. They meet discreetly in back rooms of family shops.

They denounce Arab nationalism, socialism and Western liberalism alike and call for a restored caliphate to unite all Muslims and liberate Palestine. They are politically insignificant in Uruguay, and their only leverage is the anger of a displaced generation and its diaspora contacts.

12.name: Ikhwan al-Plata
12.text:
The Brothers of the Plata are a study circle of Arab-descended students and shopkeepers in Montevideo who read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb and organise Arabic classes, Qur'an lessons and charity for poorer families of the community.

They seek a moral and religious renewal through education and social work rather than violence, and they look to the Muslim Brotherhood as a model for organising believers. Remote from Uruguayan politics, their modest leverage lies in community welfare and their links to sympathisers in Buenos Aires and São Paulo.

13.name: Oficina de Planeamiento y Presupuesto
13.text:
The Office of Planning and Budget was created by the 1967 Constitution and inherited the economists of the former Commission for Investment and Economic Development, authors of the national development plan of 1965. Attached to the presidency, it embodies the new strong executive that replaced Uruguay's collegiate government.

Its planners believe the stagnating economy needs rational management above party clientelism: budget discipline, reform of the bloated state enterprises, export promotion and investment. They are neither pachequistas nor leftists, and their leverage comes from expertise and from presidents who want answers without asking parliament.

14.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
14.text:
The Christian Democratic Party was formed in 1962 from the old Civic Union and has moved steadily to the left under Juan Pablo Terra, an architect and Catholic social thinker. It holds a few seats in parliament and has openly opposed Pacheco's emergency measures.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching, Vatican II and the communitarian ideas of Latin American Christian democracy, it calls for agrarian reform, worker participation and a third way between capitalism and communism. Its base lies among Catholic youth, teachers and professionals, and its leverage comes from its role as a bridge between the traditional parties and the left.

15.name: Asociación Rural del Uruguay
15.text:
The Rural Association of Uruguay, founded in 1871, speaks for the great cattle and sheep ranchers whose wool and beef exports earn most of the country's foreign currency. Allied with the banking and export houses of Montevideo, its members sit in ministries and boardrooms under both traditional parties.

It demands a realistic exchange rate, lower export retentions, secure property and the burial of every agrarian reform bill. Strongly anti-communist and pro-Western, it backs Pacheco's stabilisation policies, and its leverage lies in land, foreign exchange and close family ties to the political and military elite.

16.name: Lista 15
16.text:
List 15 is the Colorado faction founded by Luis Batlle Berres and led since his death in 1964 by his son Jorge Batlle Ibáñez. Once the engine of Batllista state-building, it has turned under Jorge Batlle toward free-market ideas, and it keeps an uneasy distance from Pacheco's government.

It calls for monetary stability, an open economy, less protectionism and a leaner state while defending constitutional rule. Pro-American and modernising, its base lies among Montevideo's business and professional classes, and its leverage comes from the newspaper Acción, its parliamentary bloc and the Batlle family name.

17.name: Guardianes de los Bañados
17.text:
The Guardians of the Wetlands are naturalists, birdwatchers, teachers and coastal landowners of Rocha who watch with alarm as the great wetlands of eastern Uruguay are drained for rice and pasture. They gather around the national park of Santa Teresa, the Natural History Museum and local nature societies.

They want the lagoons, palm groves and Atlantic coast protected as reserves before speculators and drainage canals destroy them. Politically marginal and without a party, their leverage lies in scientific prestige, local pride and the sympathy of a few legislators from both traditional parties.

18.name: Partido Socialista del Uruguay
18.text:
The Socialist Party of Uruguay, founded in 1910 by Emilio Frugoni, was banned by decree in December 1967 together with other left groups accused of supporting armed struggle. Under the influence of Vivián Trías it has turned from European social democracy to a Latin American, anti-imperialist and pro-Cuban socialism.

It calls for national liberation, agrarian reform, the nationalisation of banks and foreign trade, and solidarity with the Third World, rejecting both blocs' tutelage. Its base lies among intellectuals, students and some unions, and its leverage comes from its ties to the wider left and to the Tupamaros, several of whom began as Socialists.

18.name: Frente Amplio
18.text:
The Broad Front is the coalition founded on 5 February 1971 by Communists, Socialists, Christian Democrats, dissident Colorados and Blancos, and independent leftists. It has chosen General Líber Seregni, a retired constitutionalist officer, as its presidential candidate and breaks for the first time the century-old duopoly of Colorados and Blancos.

Its programme calls for agrarian reform, nationalisation of the banks and foreign trade, an end to the emergency measures and an independent foreign policy. Its leverage lies in Montevideo's unions, students and intellectuals, its rallies and the hope of an electoral path to change.

19.name: Movimiento Revolucionario Oriental
19.text:
The Eastern Revolutionary Movement was founded in 1961 by Ariel Collazo, a former Blanco deputy inspired by the Cuban Revolution. It was outlawed in December 1967 alongside the Socialists and other radical groups, and its militants now work in the shadows of the student and union movements.

It takes its line from Havana rather than Moscow or Beijing, calling for a national-revolutionary front, the expropriation of the oligarchy and continental armed struggle against imperialism. Small but energetic, its leverage lies in its Cuban connections and its links to the guerrilla underground.

20.name: Liga Federal de Acción Ruralista
20.text:
The Federal League of Ruralist Action is the agrarian protest movement built in the 1950s by the radio broadcaster Benito Nardone, whose Ruralismo carried the Blancos to power in 1958. Since Nardone's death in 1964 it has lost much of its force, but its radio audience and rural clubs survive.

It denounces Montevideo's bureaucrats, politicians and unions on behalf of the small farmer and rancher, demanding lower taxes, rural credit and hard measures against communism. Its leverage lies in rural resentment and its ability to swing votes in the interior.

21.name: Comandos de la Patria
21.text:
The Commandos of the Fatherland are the far-right shock groups that have appeared in secondary schools and the university since the upheavals of 1968, attacking left-wing students and painting slogans against communism. They are encouraged by off-duty policemen and by elements in the intelligence services frustrated with the slow fight against the Tupamaros.

They want subversion crushed by any means, the left outlawed and parliament silenced. Their numbers are small, but their leverage lies in protection from within the security forces and the fear the guerrilla war spreads among the middle classes.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas del Uruguay
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Uruguay have stayed out of politics for most of the century and remain formally subordinate to civilian rule. Yet the guerrilla war is drawing them in, a secret officers' lodge, the Tenientes de Artigas, nurtures corporate ambitions, and many officers resent politicians whom they blame for the crisis.

Officially anti-communist and trained under American programmes, the officer corps is divided between legalists, conservatives and nationalists who admire Peru's military government. For now its leverage is latent, but it rises with every Tupamaro success and every failure of the police.

23.name: Círculo Hispanista
23.text:
The Hispanist Circle is a small gathering of Catholic traditionalists, Spanish immigrants and genealogists in Montevideo who celebrate the colonial city's loyalty to the Spanish Crown. They meet in cultural societies and read the Carlist and Francoist press from Spain.

They regard the republic of parties as the source of Uruguay's decline and dream of a Catholic, hierarchical order under a crowned authority. They have no following, but their ideas circulate among a few officers and right-wing intellectuals looking for an alternative to liberal democracy.
